original_question: What physical treatment of satellite-galaxy gas stripping and subsequent star-formation shutdown is needed in semi-analytic models to avoid producing too many faint red satellites and too sparsely populated a green valley, while still matching observed satellite colour distributions?
target_in_paper: In the “Recent successes and open problems” section (page 4), semi-analytic models are described as assuming that when a galaxy is accreted onto a larger structure its hot gas reservoir is instantaneously and completely stripped (“strangulation”), causing satellites to consume their cold gas rapidly, move onto the red sequence on short timescales, and resulting in an excess of faint red satellites and an underpopulated green valley (L172–L179).
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the need to revise the modelling of gas stripping and star-formation quenching in satellite galaxies within semi-analytic models to avoid the overproduction of faint red satellites and underpopulation of the green valley, and to better match observed satellite colour distributions.
missing_details: Definition of “strangulation” as the instantaneous and complete removal of the hot gas reservoir upon satellite infall
Specification that this stripping occurs at virial crossing/accretion onto a larger halo
Reference to hydrodynamical simulation results of McCarthy et al. (2008) showing partial hot halo retention
Mention of the implementation by Font et al. (2008) in the Durham semi-analytic model
Clarification that the question seeks a prescription for hot gas stripping timescales or efficiencies
Identification of the observational metrics: satellite colour distribution, green-valley population, and faint red satellite counts
refined_question: In the context of modern semi-analytic galaxy formation models—where satellite galaxies undergo instantaneous, complete removal of their hot gas reservoir (“strangulation”) upon accretion, leading to an excess of faint red satellites and a sparsely populated green valley—what specific prescription for hot gas stripping timescales and efficiencies (e.g., those derived from high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations by McCarthy et al. 2008 and implemented by Font et al. 2008 in the Durham model) is required to slow star-formation quenching and reproduce the observed satellite colour distribution?
justification: The refined question directly echoes the paper’s description in “Recent successes and open problems” (page 4, L172–L179), specifying the instantaneous stripping assumption (“strangulation”), its consequences for satellite colours, and invoking the hydrodynamical simulation and semi-analytic model modifications cited immediately thereafter (L180–L185). It incorporates all necessary definitions, context, and references to make the question self-contained and faithful to the paper’s intent.
